source.instrument: NIST IR 8286A r1, Identifying and Estimating Cybersecurity Risk for Enterprise Risk Management
source.sections: s 2.3.1 Selecting Risk Analysis Methodologies; s 2.3.2 Techniques for Estimating Likelihood and Impact

note: The catalogue is DATA, not logic. `nistSays` is quoted VERBATIM from the locator beside it and is never paraphrased — an entry NIST does not discuss carries no `nistSays` at all rather than an invented one. `requires` and `visibilityWhy` are CAC's own words, derived from the quote, and are marked as such by living in different fields: nothing in this file attributes CAC's derivation to NIST.
visibilityNote: `checkable` means every prerequisite this method needs is a fact the register itself holds, so an unmet one can be flagged from the file alone. `external` means the method's real prerequisites live in the analyst's workbook, their priors or their branch probabilities — none of which this toolkit can see. An `external` method NEVER emits `method-prerequisite-unmet`: flagging the absence of something we cannot look at would assert a fact about work done outside the toolkit. Same restraint as `untraced` being a value rather than a gap.
licensingNote: Open FAIR and IEC 31010:2019 are third-party standards under licence. They are named and cited so a reader can find them, and NOT ONE WORD of their text is reproduced here — including the passages NIST itself quotes. Where a licensed source and NIST make the same point, this file carries NIST's public-domain sentence instead. Nothing in this catalogue requires buying a licence to read.
scopeNote: This toolkit does not EXECUTE any of these methods and never will — see NIST's own footnote 29 at s 2.3.2, quoted on the `sme-estimation` entry. Advising that Monte Carlo fits, and that it needs software this toolkit does not provide, is the opposite of scope creep.

methods.label: Subject matter expert estimation
requires: named experts
a record of who estimated and when
methods.nistSays: Some analysis techniques are based on estimates from subject matter experts' (SMEs) experience and knowledge. Some methods, such as this SME estimation, can be subjective.
methods.nistScopeCaveat: It is the intention of this document to introduce the reader to commonly used estimation techniques. The authors defer to other industry resources for comprehensive details regarding how to perform such analyses.
methods.visibilityWhy: The register holds the estimator's name and the date on the method record itself.

methods.label: Delphi exercise
requires: a panel of estimators
more than one round
responses not attributable between rounds
methods.nistNames: Named by NIST inside a worked example — "A poll of the security leaders (using a Delphi exercise) determined that there is a 50 to 70 % chance that the payroll system will be attacked" — and not otherwise described. No NIST statement of its requirements or limitations exists to quote, so none is claimed.
methods.visibilityWhy: The rounds, the panel and the anonymity between rounds all happen outside the register. Nothing here can tell a Delphi exercise from a single conversation somebody labelled one.

methods.label: Estimation from knowledge of prior events
requires: a loss history
events comparable to the one being estimated
methods.nistSays: While past performance is not a guarantee of future probability, it provides some information that helps inform likelihood estimates.
methods.visibilityWhy: The register holds this organisation's risks, not its incident history. Whether the prior events used were comparable is a judgement made outside it.

methods.label: Three-point estimation
requires: an optimistic, most-likely and pessimistic value
ideally more than one estimator polled
methods.nistSays: This method, illustrated in Fig. 14, is useful because it considers the judgment of available SMEs.
methods.nistLimitation: Notably, the level of effort for estimating risk factors increases with the required level of rigor.
methods.nistBiasCaution: For better estimates of O, M, and P and to eliminate bias, the estimator should poll multiple SMEs and determine the average of individual O values, M values, and P values before proceeding with the three-point estimate.
methods.visibilityWhy: The three values are not stored. Storing them is BL-86, parked on migration cost — until then the register cannot see whether an estimate had three points or one.

methods.label: Event tree analysis
methods.typeWhy: NIST states it can be run either way, so this catalogue does not pin it to one. The `type` recorded on the risk is the analyst's declaration, not a lookup from here.
requires: an initiating threat event
a branch structure of outcomes
for the quantitative form, a probability per branch
methods.nistSays: Event Tree Analysis (ETA) is a graphical technique that helps practitioners evaluate the downstream impact of a given scenario (as determined in Sec.2.2.4).
methods.nistLimitation: A qualitative approach would still describe the Yes/No conditions and outcomes but would not include specific probabilities of each branch.
methods.visibilityWhy: The branch probabilities live in the analyst's tree. The register holds one likelihood and one impact and cannot see the structure behind them.

methods.label: Monte Carlo simulation
requires: distributions for the input variables
simulation software this toolkit does not provide
methods.nistSays: While expert judgement is valuable in estimating risk parameters, one way to reduce subjectivity is to supplement that judgement using simulation models.
methods.nistLimitation: Simulation is not always necessary, but with the variables for considering likelihood and impact values (based on the factors described in Sec.2.2), randomly sampled probabilities can help identify a range of possible values.
methods.visibilityWhy: The simulation, its cycles and its input distributions are all outside the register. A recorded exposure figure looks identical whether it came from several hundred thousand cycles or from a guess.

methods.label: Bayesian analysis
requires: a distribution model
a set of known prior data
methods.nistSays: Bayesian analysis describes methods for considering conditional probability - applying a distribution model and a set of known prior data to help estimate the probability of a future outcome.
methods.nistScopeCaveat: Application and usage of Bayesian analysis is outside the scope of this document but is included here as a valid quantitative means for performing risk analysis estimation.
methods.visibilityWhy: The priors are the method. They are not in the register, and a prior nobody wrote down is indistinguishable here from one carefully chosen.

methods.label: Estimation workshops
requires: a small team
assumptions recorded so they can be challenged
methods.nistSays: utilize small teams to collaborate and challenge assumptions, anchor estimates in real-world analogies and ensure logical consistency. These sessions also reduce individual bias and increase shared understanding of scenarios and inputs.
methods.supplementaryWhy: NIST lists this as an organizational process that SUPPLEMENTS an estimation technique, not as a technique on its own: "organizations are encouraged to utilize the following organizational processes to supplement the estimation techniques" (s 2.3.2).
methods.visibilityWhy: Whether a workshop happened, and who was in it, is not a fact the register holds.

methods.label: Calibration training and assessment
requires: estimators trained and assessed for calibration
methods.nistSays: this process improves individuals' ability to estimate uncertainty accurately. Techniques such as the equivalent bet test (e.g., "Would you bet $100 that the true value falls within this range?") help improve probabilistic thinking and reduce overconfidence.
methods.supplementaryWhy: Listed by NIST among the organizational processes that supplement the estimation techniques (s 2.3.2).
methods.visibilityWhy: Whether an estimator has been calibrated is a fact about a person, held nowhere in this file.

methods.label: Sensitivity analysis
requires: a model with input assumptions that can be varied
methods.nistSays: not just of the model, but of the input assumptions-used to identify which uncertain factors most affect the output. This guides analysts to focus effort where it matters most and improves decision-maker confidence that uncertainty has been appropriately scoped. Sensitivity analysis can also help with setting escalation thresholds for KRIs and may suggest new metrics to monitor.
methods.supplementaryWhy: Listed by NIST among the organizational processes that supplement the estimation techniques (s 2.3.2).
methods.visibilityWhy: The model and its assumptions are outside the register.

methods.label: Tracking actuals versus forecasts
requires: historical estimates kept
realized outcomes to compare them against
methods.nistSays: a discipline common in finance but rarely applied in cybersecurity. By comparing historical estimates to realized outcomes over time, organizations can improve estimation accuracy and identify where assumptions consistently under- or over-shoot.
methods.supplementaryWhy: Listed by NIST among the organizational processes that supplement the estimation techniques (s 2.3.2).
methods.visibilityWhy: The register keeps its own history, but the realized outcomes to compare against are incidents, and those live in incident-materiality.

methods.label: Open FAIR
requires: the Open Group's Risk Taxonomy standard
loss magnitude and frequency estimates
methods.nistNames: NIST cites "The Open Group Standard for Risk Taxonomy (O-RT) Version 3.0.1, part of the Open Factor Analysis of Information Risk (OpenFAIR) series of documents" and quotes it. That quotation is NOT reproduced here.
methods.visibilityWhy: Its factors are computed in the analyst's own model. The register sees a resulting score and nothing behind it.
methods.namingRule: A FAIR analysis missing part of the taxonomy is `open-fair` at `conformance: partial` with the deviation stated. It is never renamed to a coined variant such as "FAIR-lite": renaming a licensed third-party standard to describe a reduced version of it is a false claim about somebody else's work.

methods.label: IEC 31010:2019 risk assessment techniques
methods.typeWhy: It is a catalogue of techniques rather than a single method.
requires: the standard itself, which is licensed
methods.nistNames: NIST cites "International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standard 31010:2019, Risk management - Risk assessment techniques" as providing a comprehensive list of risk analysis techniques, and quotes a passage from it. That quotation is NOT reproduced here. Where the licensed text and NIST make the same point about data quality, this catalogue carries NIST's own public-domain sentence instead, on the `dataDependency` note below.
methods.visibilityWhy: Not a method this register can hold prerequisites for.

dataDependency.nistSays: Unfortunately, without supporting data, well-intentioned but misguided methods of risk analysis amount to little more than a guess.
dataDependency.why: This is the sentence behind v1 check 1. A register declaring quantitative analysis with no currency recorded has not written down the unit its numbers are in.

selectionCriteria.note: What `suggest-method` reads, quoted VERBATIM from NIST IR 8286A r1 s 2.3.1. These are criteria to weigh, not a ranking, and this catalogue produces no score.

criteria.nistSays: there are benefits to both qualitative and quantitative risk analysis methodologies and even the use of multiple methodologies, based on enterprise strategy, organization preference, and data availability
When selecting a risk assessment technique, organizations should consider the analysis costs in light of the desired outcome to help determine the most cost-effective technique.
Inexpensive but accurate qualitative analysis that identifies the most risks and leads to best mitigating those risks may be the right move for a particular organization.

For others, a highly detailed quantitative risk assessment may require more resources than a qualitative approach but may also provide specific and actionable information that helps to focus attention on important threat scenarios.
Quantitatively informed qualitative decision-making should be the objective in the absence of purely quantitative-driven decisions.
